journal: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management
t: Green fuels and emerging business models for sustainable logistics: decoding innovation for the genesis of new supply chains
a: Purpose Anchored on social exchange theory/transition management theory and seeking to contribute to the study on sustainable business model innovation, the present investigation analyses the difficulties and opportunities faced by a company focused on biomethane production as it develops its supply chain. In that path, we address key issues linked to the structuration of a new and complex operation, including securing financing, accessing agricultural waste, distributing biomethane and manufacturing biomethane-powered trucks. Ultimately, the study aims to provide new and useful knowledge for the development of a more environmentally performant logistics at a business model level. Design/methodology/approach Two factorial scenario-based behavioural experiments were conducted with a total sample of 345 respondents from the United States to evaluate professionals' openness to supporting a commercial biomethane project based on trust, attitude towards the firm and corporate image. We also assess potential reputational benefits for supply chain partners based on consumer perceptions on the same variables and purchase intention. Findings Results indicate that the truck manufacturers group rated the biomethane company higher than the other groups, suggesting that they would be much more probable partners – in opposition to fuel distributors, who seem to remain less positive about the perspective partnership. Data also suggest that partnering with a company on a sustainable-oriented project has a positive reputational effect, as related benefits were found for the sugar mill, fuel distributor and truck manufacturer. This indicates that investing in green logistics can yield positive reputational impacts. Practical implications The study anticipates some of the main challenges and potential upsides characteristic of ventures of this nature, offering valuable data for those interested in advancing green logistics through sustainable business model innovation. It highlights the importance of behavioural and reputational aspects in forming partnerships that can help scale biomethane production and reduce diesel use in transportation. Originality/value This study is dedicated to understanding the development of a highly complex business model, linking innovation in sustainable logistics with the organisation of the means that enable its implementation. Although not an empirical case study per se, the fact that it is based on real developments bring the analysis closer to the situations faced by companies in practice. Outcomes add to the further comprehension of the dynamics of multi-stakeholder governance.
k: biomethane; green logistics; sustainable business model innovation; supply chain development; social exchange theory; corporate reputation; trust; purchase intention; stakeholder collaboration; agricultural waste; fuel distribution; multi-stakeholder governance

journal: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Insights
t: Exploring travel, technology adoption and its outcomes among senior travellers
a: Purpose This study explores facets of older adults' leisure travel behaviour, examining their motives for technology adoption during travel and the role of technology in shaping their travel experiences. It also assesses the outcomes of both leisure travel and travel-related technology adoption for this cohort. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was adopted in which older adults aged 60 years upwards were recruited through purposive sampling, ensuring distribution in demographic variables like gender and living status. Twenty semi-structured interviews were conducted, and data were analysed using Braun et al. (2016) thematic analysis method. Findings Three themes were constructed from the narratives, namely: “readiness” (travel readiness and technology readiness), “technology use during travel” (related to travel behaviour and decision-making) and “outcome realisation of travel and technology use”. Generally, it is observed that older adults who use digital tools for planning and trip engagement benefit from safe, personalised and comfortable tourism experiences that enhance their sense of purpose and general well-being. Practical implications As the tourism experience plays a significant role in promoting optimal aging, tourism destinations and practitioners should consider the typical characteristics of senior tourists to develop user-friendly technology products in the tourism industry. Originality/value The study provides nuanced qualitative insights into how older adults integrate technology into their leisure travel experiences and the outcomes of such interactions on well-being. It expands the intersectionality of aging, tourism and technology use for meaningful interventions at service provider and policy levels.

t: Bias in Securities Litigation Event Studies When Volatility and Beta Shift
a: Traditional event study methodology can lead to erroneous conclusions—incorrect identification of an insignificant price change as statistically significant (and vice versa)—when there are volatility shifts, and the model is estimated from a prior low volatility period. Earlier studies have used the empirical distribution of the test statistic to adjust for the fatter tails created due to volatility shifts. We show that the empirical distribution approach (EDA) can only account for a shift in volatility and leads to biased results when there is a simultaneous shift in the beta. We propose using a regime switching (RS) model to estimate beta and volatility for different regimes. We show that using regime-specific beta and volatility removes the bias in excess returns caused by estimating the parameters from a prior period, with different beta and volatility. Our findings have practical implications for securities litigation, where event studies serve as key evidence. We highlight the need for re-evaluating excess return methodologies in high volatility environments and provide a framework for improving event study robustness in legal and regulatory contexts.
k: securities litigation; event study; volatility shifts; beta-shifts; regime switching; abnormal returns; parameter estimation bias

journal: Revue Internationale de Psychosociologie et de Gestion des Comportements Organisationnels (ripco)
t: Diriger par la confiance : les compétences émotionnelles au cœur de la construction d’un climat de confiance
a: Dans un environnement incertain et complexe, la confiance émerge comme un déterminant crucial de la performance et de la pérennité organisationnelles. La capacité des dirigeants à créer un climat de confiance revêt ainsi un caractère stratégique indispensable pour les entreprises. En ce sens, l’objectif de notre article est donc d’étudier comment les compétences émotionnelles des dirigeants favorisent-elles la création d’un climat de confiance ? Pour cela, nous avons mené une étude qualitative à travers 30 entretiens semi-directifs individuels avec des interlocuteurs exerçant des fonctions de direction. Nos principaux résultats mettent en lumière comment les compétences émotionnelles individuelles des dirigeants peuvent, à travers trois mécanismes convergents, générer des effets systémiques sur l’organisation dans son ensemble créant ainsi un climat organisationnel de confiance.

t: Statistical causality and identification between filtrations
a: The concepts of identification and strong identification among σ-algebras are introduced in Florens et al. [Elements of Bayesian statistics, New York: Marcel Dekker; 1990. (Pure and applied mathematics: a series of monographs and textbooks)]. In this paper we propose generalization of these definitions for information represented by filtrations (i.e., by σ-algebra families). Then, we prove that identification and strong identification are directly connected to the concept of statistical causality (based on Granger's definition of causality). Also, we apply some of this results on general reduced Bayesian experiment.

t: Matching for impact: a dyadic process model of mentor–venture alignment in entrepreneurial support organizations
a: Business incubators and accelerators (BIAs) play a central role in regional entrepreneurial ecosystems by providing mentoring to support new venture development, yet mentoring outcomes vary considerably. While prior research documents mentoring benefits, limited attention has been paid to how mentors and ventures are matched or how these processes shape outcomes. This study conceptualizes mentor–venture matching as a dyadic, co-constructed process and examines how alignment between mentors and ventures shapes the formation and evolution mentoring relationships and their outcomes. Drawing on a multi-stage qualitative research design involving interviews with program managers, twenty mentors, and twenty-one new ventures across twelve Belgian BIAs, as well as follow-up interviews with ventures, the study identifies distinct yet complementary selection criteria on both sides of the dyad. Mentors evaluate ventures based on experiential alignment, deep-level personal characteristics, and venture-specific attributes, whereas ventures assess mentors based on expertise, interpersonal qualities, and value alignment. The findings show that alignment across these dimensions is associated with different mentoring outcomes, ranging from short-term problem solving to access to networks, investment opportunities, and long-term professional collaborations. This study develops a process model explaining how early-stage matching conditions shape the depth, durability, and strategic value of mentoring relationships over time. By linking matching processes to differentiated outcomes, the study advances a dyadic perspective on entrepreneurial mentoring and contributes to research on entrepreneurial ecosystems by demonstrating how BIAs act as intermediaries shaping how mentoring relationships influence access to resources within entrepreneurial ecosystems.
k: entrepreneurship mentoring; business incubators; accelerators; entrepreneurial ecosystems; mentoring outcomes; startups; value alignment; network access; access to resources

journal: International Journal of Business Competition and Growth
t: The tetrapreneur model of Indonesias halal-certified coffee exports to the Egyptian market
a: : This study applies the tetrapreneur model comprising chainpreneur, marketpreneur, qualitypreneur, and brandpreneur dimensions to assess and enhance Indonesias halal-certified coffee exports to Egypt, a promising yet underdeveloped market. Using a qualitative case study approach, in-depth interviews were conducted with eight key business actors: four Indonesian exporters and four Egyptian importers. The findings reveal critical gaps in Indonesias export performance, including inefficient supply chains, limited market intelligence, low investment, and weak national branding. In contrast, Egyptian importers exhibit stronger digital capabilities, responsiveness, and brand collaboration. The study proposes a strategic matrix to address these issues through supply chain digitalisation, improved market intelligence, Robusta foam-quality standardisation, and national co-branding initiatives. As the first to use the tetrapreneur model in halal-certified coffee trade, this research offers a novel framework for evaluating entrepreneurial capacity and export readiness. Practical recommendations target exporters, policymakers, and certification bodies to support sustainable, value-added trade between Indonesia and Egypt.

t: Measuring measurement error
a: We collect 2,848 instrumental variable (IV) regressions from 391 papers published in top economics and finance journals and show that estimated IV coefficients are often much larger than their OLS counterparts, even when theory suggests they should be smaller. We derive meta-regression estimators that distinguish measurement error bias from omitted variable bias and simultaneity bias; applying our estimators to a set of 1,040 comparable regressions from 139 papers, we find that measurement error shrinks reported coefficients by about two to four times. Measurement error remains quantitatively important even after accounting for weak instruments, publication bias, instrument invalidity, and heterogeneous treatment effects. Our results suggest that measurement error is a severe, pervasive, and understated source of bias in economics and finance.
k: measurement error; instrumental variable estimation; measurement error bias; omitted variable bias; simultaneity bias; weak instruments; publication bias; assessment validity; treatment effect heterogeneity; econometric bias

t: The Profit Split Method across Jurisdictions – Report on Ireland
a: Ireland’s transfer pricing legislation does not prescribe a hierarchy of methods and instead requires taxpayers to select the most appropriate method in accordance with the OECD Guidelines. While the profit split method (PSM) can be applied as the primary method where unique and valuable contributions are made by multiple parties, taxpayers should be prepared to justify its selection over simpler methods. As illustrated in the case study, the PSM can also serve as a valuable corroborative method in competent authority matters, providing additional comfort on the appropriateness of profit allocations. This article is part of a special issue of the International Transfer Pricing Journal on the application of the PSM across jurisdictions. The other articles include the General Report and contributions on Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Korea, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and the United States.
k: profit split method; transfer pricing; Ireland; OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines; method selection; profit distribution; multinational corporations

t: A collaborative autoethnography of embodied leadership struggles: The case of leaderful practices in a university context
a: This study explores embodied leadership struggles and the ongoing negotiation of leaderful practices in a university context. The empirical material is based on autoethnographic diary notes of two authors of this study. Through our collaborative analysis, we identify two themes of embodied leadership struggles as we attempted to create leaderful practices in the university setting: (1) moving between heroic and collective leadership expectations through bodily spaces and (2) while attempting to navigate our vulnerability in relation to our leadership expectations about the quest to find leaderful practices . Our study makes three contributions. First, our study contributes to the discussion of leadership-as-practice (L-A-P) by articulating the embodied struggles managers face when attempting to enact and promote leaderful practices. Second, the study contributes to the understanding of how these struggles can become a source of leadership learning through vulnerability. Rather than treating vulnerability as an inherently empowering personal condition, we show that vulnerability is a context-dependent, relationally shaped, and negotiated phenomenon. Finally, our study offers a methodological contribution by advancing collaborative autoethnography as a means for enacting leadership learning.
k: embodied leadership; leadership as practice; vulnerability; leadership learning; heroic leadership; shared leadership; university administration; bodily space; collaborative autoethnography; leadership expectations

t: AI-mediated plausibility regimes: Entrepreneurial judgment, epistemic risk, and the distribution of entrepreneurial futures
a: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely portrayed as enhancing entrepreneurial decision-making through improved prediction, pattern recognition, and data-driven evaluation. Yet entrepreneurship frequently unfolds under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, where action depends on entrepreneurial judgment about uncertain and evolving futures rather than calculable prediction alone. We theorize how AI-based systems reshape the epistemic conditions under which entrepreneurial beliefs are formed and evaluated. We argue that AI systems are not epistemically neutral: by generating plausibility signals from historical data, they influence which ventures appear credible and worthy of support. We conceptualize these dynamics as AI-mediated plausibility regimes and identify a dual epistemic risk. In generative modes, AI may inflate evaluative confidence beyond what the available epistemic grounding warrants (false positives). In evaluative and screening modes, AI may disadvantage low-precedent but potentially transformative ventures (false negatives). By distinguishing these system classes and their distributional effects, we specify when AI may expand entrepreneurial imagination and when it may narrow entrepreneurial variety.
k: entrepreneurial judgment; Knightian uncertainty; epistemic risk; false positives and false negatives

t: Time variation of size premium in the options market
a: : Many studies show that equity premiums, including the size premium, tend to intensify in bad economic states, as investors demand higher compensation for risk in turmoil. In contrast, this paper documents a surprising finding that the size premium in the options market strengthens in good economic states. In the full sample, equity options of small firms underperform those of large firms; however, this underperformance disappears in economic downturns and becomes more pronounced in upturns. This finding contrasts with the time-varying risk-return trade-off but is consistent with the demand-based option pricing theory. Particularly, in downturns, high demand for safe assets lowers the demand for small and speculative firms’ options, making these options less expensive and attenuating the underperformance of small firms’ options. Practitioners seeking to exploit the size premium in the options market should direct their trading toward upturns rather than downturns to enhance performance.
k: size premium; equity options; small business; economic downturn; economic upturn; risk-return tradeoff; option pricing

journal: Scandinavian Journal of Hospitality and Tourism
t: From forests to saunas: everyday urban wellness practices and their tourism potential in cities. A qualitative exploration of holistic well-being
a: This qualitative, exploratory study examines how urban-dwelling Finns sustain holistic well-being and how these everyday practices can inform tourism marketing and urban planning. Grounded in Dunn’s [Dunn, H. L. (1959). High-Level Wellness for Man and Society. American Journal of Public Health and the Nations Health, 49(6), 786–792. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.49.6.786] body–mind–spirit model and Baer and Gesler’s [Baer, L. D., & Gesler, W. M. (2004). Reconsidering the concept of therapeutic landscapes in J D Salinger's The Catcher in the Rye. Area, 36(4), 404–413. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0004-0894.2004.00240.x] therapeutic landscape framework, the research analyses how natural, built, social, and symbolic environments support urban wellness. Data were collected from focus groups in Espoo and Turku (n = 13) and specialist interviews with destination management organisations and urban planners (n = 4). The findings show that Finnish urban wellness is deeply rooted in nearby forests and parks, strong social ties, locally produced food, and regular sauna use. Both cities emphasise sustainability, nature stewardship, and community well-being, despite differing institutional roles. The results also indicate that many resident well-being practices are routine-based and culturally embedded, meaning they do not automatically translate into tourism offerings and must be considered selectively and contextually. Although the small sample limits generalisability, the study provides valuable insight into the lived experience of urban well-being. It contributes to wellness tourism literature by illustrating how urban environments may serve as wellness destinations that support both resident and visitor well-being when development aligns carefully with local needs, environmental limits, and everyday practices.
k: wellness tourism; holistic well-being; therapeutic landscapes; sauna use; social ties; local food; urban planning; tourism marketing; Finnish cities

t: The value of a statistical life year
a: Embedded in the value of a statistical life (VSL) is a stream of valuations of each expected year of life. The value of a statistical life year (VSLY) has a policy-relevant role analogous to the VSL, except that it monetizes risks to short periods of life extension. This article reviews previous studies and reports new labor market estimates of the average VSLY and the variation of these values with age using two methods—inferring the average VSLY based on estimates of the VSL and a new method that provides direct empirical estimates of the valuation of a discounted life year. The direct estimates of the VSLY yield larger values than the constructed estimates. The VSLY based on fatality rates by industry and occupation is $600,000 to $800,000 at a 3% interest rate. Estimates based on age-adjusted fatality rates are somewhat lower. The discount rate used in assessing the VSLY has a pivotal effect on the estimated VSLY. The VSLY is substantially lower in the absence of discounting and more than doubled at a discount rate of 10%. Failure to use a positive discount rate greatly understates the VSLY. The article also reviews previous VSLY studies as well as estimates of the discount rate for years of life expectancy.
k: value of a statistical life year; value of a statistical life; discount rate; occupational fatality rates; risk valuation

journal: International Journal of Environment and Pollution
t: Impact of sewage treatment plants on local tourism and ecotourism
a: Sewage treatment plants (STP) significantly impact local tourism and ecotourism by improving water quality, enhancing scenic accessibility, and boosting tourist experiences.This study analysed STP effects in Xi'an, comparing suspended solids and tourism revenue in four scenic areas in June 2023 and June 2025.Results showed STP reduced suspended solids, improved environmental quality, and increased tourism revenue.Specifically, scenic areas exhibited notable decreases in water pollutants and substantial increases in income.STP supports ecosystem protection, enhances tourism resources, and promotes sustainable development.This highlights STP's role in balancing environmental protection and tourism growth, offering insights for sustainable ecotourism strategies.
k: wastewater treatment plants; ecotourism; local tourism; tourism revenue; suspended solids; water quality; tourist attractions; environmental protection; sustainable tourism; Xi'an

t: What Goes Up May Come Down: Trends in the Upward and Downward Occupational Mobility of U.S. Workers
a: This paper estimates annual upward and downward occupational mobility rates in the United States between 2018 and 2024. The authors find that only 6.6% of workers in the lowest-quality occupations moved into higher-quality occupations. Conversely, 8.0% of workers in middle-quality occupations moved into lower-quality occupations. To capture trends, the authors estimate annual mobility rates from 2011 onward and find increasing downward mobility through 2018 and increasing upward mobility through 2019. In both series, higher variability was found but little change comparing 2018 and 2024. The authors use multinomial logit regressions to estimate individual characteristics associated with upward and downward occupational mobility. Higher levels of education and younger age are associated with increased transitions to higher-quality occupations and reduced downward occupational transitions. The authors find mixed results for race, ethnicity, and gender, with results suggesting the importance of human capital investments and other interventions that promote upward mobility and may prevent downward mobility.
k: occupational mobility; upward mobility; downward mobility; occupational quality; labour market transitions; human capital; age; race and ethnicity; gender; mobility trends

t: Epilogue
a: Dr. Robert W. Proctor was a prolific writer, and he collaborated with numerous researchers across both basic and applied areas of psychology. Dr. Proctor's curriculum vitae listed more than 180 coauthors for his journal publications alone. Moreover, he was the major advisor for 35 PhD students and three postdoctoral fellows. The number of research collaborators and former students, and the range of research topics he published on, made it difficult for us to select potential contributors for the special issue. Thus, we relied mainly on The American Journal of Psychology's call for papers to solicit submissions to the special issue. As we discussed in the preface (Vu & Schneider, 2026) to the first of what ended up being two special issues, the goal was to celebrate the contributions of Dr. Proctor as a complete psychologist who made significant contributions to both basic and applied research.Dr. Proctor often remarked that he liked studying stimulus–response compatibility effects because they are simple yet effective in allowing researchers to examine the mechanisms underlying perception–action relations. Compatibility effects reveal the representations (e.g., types of codes: spatial vs. verbal, horizontal vs. vertical) and reference frames (e.g., horizontal vs. vertical, internal vs. external) used to link perception and action (see Proctor & Vu, 2006; Proctor & Cho, 2006). Several articles in the special issue examine the nature of spatial coding and the role of reference frames. Lee and Cho showed that different spatial codes were used for the processing of horizontal and vertical gaze directions. Specifically, horizontal gaze direction was associated with processing of visuospatial attributes, and vertical gaze direction was associated with the processing of semantic–spatial attributes. Tomko and Schneider showed that the visual dominance effect (conflicting visual–spatial information substantially impairs responses to auditory–spatial stimuli, whereas conflicting auditory–spatial information has a weaker influence on responding to visual–spatial stimuli) occurred primarily in spatial tasks with physical location stimuli but not with verbal stimuli. Warren et al. showed that the administration of vibrotactile stimuli on the body invokes a tendency for coding using an internal frame but that an external reference frame is also used based on the task context. These studies continue to use congruity effects to reveal how perception is translated into action.Compatibility effects also reveal natural versus learned response tendencies (Proctor & Vu, 2010). Natural ones are universal in that they are based on interactions with the natural environment, where spatial relations are similar for everyone. Learned response tendencies differ between groups of individuals because they are developed through experiences with unique display–control relations. t: Realigning the dots: the disconnect between student assessment practice and learning in entrepreneurship education
a: In the evolving field of entrepreneurship education (EE), the pivotal role of student assessment received limited attention on the research and practice front. While significant strides have been made in pedagogical practices, assessment methods have not adequately evolved to fully support entrepreneurial learning outcomes. The ‘assessment-learning’ alignment is important because students confine their learning to match the assessment criteria, which can undermine the effectiveness of entrepreneurship education. Drawing upon the theory of constructive alignment, we seek to answer the question of how student assessment is aligned with the intended learning outcomes in experiential EE. Utilising multiple methodological approaches – including focus group discussions, surveys, and analyses of course descriptors – we gathered data from students, educators, and other stakeholders across 14 higher education institutions in Ireland. The findings reveal that current assessment practices in EE are grade-oriented and provide less feedback, which disconnects the students from entrepreneurial learning. By emphasising the need for a feedback-oriented assessment framework, this research shows that alignment between ‘assessment-learning’ and feedback-focused assessment is essential to complement entrepreneurial learning.
k: entrepreneurship education; student assessment; constructive alignment; experiential learning; university teaching

journal: Career Development and Transition for Exceptional Individuals
t: Utility of the Vocational Fit Assessment and VocFit Data Reports: A Mixed-Methods Study
a: The use of evidence-based assessments is an important part of the transition-planning process for high school students with disabilities. However, few assessments inform vocational decision-making. The Vocational Fit Assessment (VFA) and VocFit data reports inform such decisions by providing an integrated assessment of worker abilities and job demands. There is a need to explore VFA and VocFit utility. This mixed-methods convergent parallel study surveyed professional users (e.g., teachers, job coaches, therapists, administrators) of the VFA and VocFit data reports ( N = 104). Deductive thematic analyses were used to identify themes in open-ended responses, which were integrated with quantitative results from Likert-type responses. More than 90% of participants agreed the VFA was appropriate, accessible, and acceptable for supporting transition to employment. Participants commented that VocFit data reports provide visualizations that make sharing data easy. Approximately 90% of participants found the VFA and VocFit data reports relevant and effective; many offered suggestions for improvement. Roughly 80% agreed that the VFA and VocFit data reports were practicable, indicating a need to clarify administration materials. The study supports the clinical utility of the VFA and VocFit data reports and identifies several areas to improve the tools, including changes to VFA items and the rating scale to enhance usability. Qualitative data revealed that users may not use the tools as intended, further emphasizing the need for greater implementation fidelity to maximize benefits for young adults in transition to employment.
k: career choice; school-to-work transition; students with disabilities; high school students; implementation fidelity; job coaches; transition planning

t: Does climate stabilization mean the end of economic growth? A critical assessment of the degrowth hypothesis
a: Prominent degrowth scholars claim that sustained economic degrowth in wealthy nations is a viable strategy, necessary condition, and/or inevitable outcome in efforts to address climate change. These claims—referred to here as the ‘degrowth hypothesis’—rest on two core arguments. First, societies cannot decouple CO₂ emissions from GDP quickly enough without degrowth. Second, renewable energy resources cannot sustain continued growth. This paper assesses these claims through a mixed-methods approach, including critical literature review, scenario analysis, and analytical modeling. The findings challenge all three claims. On viability, the scenario analysis reveals that achieving even zero growth globally is not possible without severely limiting growth in the Global South; even then, Global North economies must contract at least 50% by 2050. In less politically infeasible scenarios—where only the Global North pursues zero or slow degrowth, still requiring the dismantling of growth-based capitalism—the global economy continues growing 2.2%—2.5% annually, yielding only marginal emissions benefits. On necessity, degrowth scholars tend to overstate required decoupling rates while understating what aggressive renewable energy and energy efficiency programs can achieve. On inevitability, the claim that renewable energy cannot sustain growth relies on flawed interpretations of the energy return on investment (EROI) and is contradicted empirically.
k: degrowth; climate stabilization; economic growth; renewable energy; energy return on investment; energy efficiency; Global South; climate change mitigation; economic contraction

t: Effects of income diversification on the stability of Southeast Asian banks in the context of digital transformation of the economy
a: Purpose This study aims to examine and estimate the impact of the transformation of banking operations from traditional banking to digital banking and income diversification on the stability of banks in Southeast Asian countries during the period from 2006 to 2021. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a Bayesian model to examine the impact of digital transformation (represented by the variables: BIS: Number of broadband internet subscribers, in thousands; and MB100: Number of mobile phone subscribers, per 100 people LN) along with bank income diversification represented by (LA: Bank liquid assets compared to deposits and short-term capital sources; and NII: Bank non-interest income compared to total income, in percent) on the stability of banks (represented by ZCORE: Z-score of the banking system). Data are taken from 2006 to 2021 at annual frequency in 10 countries: Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, East Timor, Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam. In addition, the study also conducts a robustness test of the research model through the use of ordinary least squares, fixed effects model, random effects model and feasible generalized least squares models. Findings When banks diversify their non-interest income, it creates positive effects on bank stability by reducing their dependence on traditional credit business activities, which contain many potential risks. However, the banking sector of Southeast Asian countries is in the early stages of digital transformation, so the cost of digitalization creates great pressure on financial capital flows and causes weakening of bank stability. Practical implications Cost is an issue that needs to be considered for the digital transformation process of banks. Banks can take advantage of technologies and technology transfer activities from advanced countries to shorten the time and reduce costs for the digitalization process of business activities. National development policies need to aim at equipping modern technology infrastructure to create an advanced ecosystem to support the digital transformation activities of banks. Banks need to integrate income diversification and digital transformation to aim for stable and sustainable development in the long term. Originality/value This study provides empirical evidence on the dual impact of income diversification and digital transformation on the stability of Southeast Asian banks. The study proposes several recommendations for policymakers to aim at achieving stable and sustainable growth for banks in Southeast Asia.
k: bank stability; income diversification; digital transformation; digital banking; non-interest income; Z-score; broadband internet subscribers; mobile phone subscribers; banking regulation

journal: International Journal of Work Organisation and Emotion
t: The Synergy of Emotional Intelligence and Leadership Styles: A pathway to Positive Workplace Outcomes
a: The ever-evolving concept 'emotional intelligence' (EI), has gained a prominent attention in the modern workplace with its significant capability to predict positive workplace outcomes in the workplace and organisational success. The emotional intelligence characteristics such as acknowledging, understanding, regulating and managing emotions helps the individuals to an improved performance in the workplace, which will ultimately lead to the workplace success. The present study addresses the influence of the emotional intelligence and leadership styles adopted by them on the workplace outcome of college teachers, particularly in Kerala. The results of the structural equation modelling (SEM) performed reveals that, emotional intelligence exerts a strong as well as a significant influence on the leadership styles adopted by the teachers as well as they exerts a significant influence on the workplace outcomes of college teachers such as job performance (JP), job satisfaction (JS).
k: emotional intelligence; leadership styles; workplace outcomes; employee performance; job satisfaction; college teachers; teacher leadership; emotion regulation; Kerala

t: How Destination Familiarity Influences American Millennials’ Preference for Culturally Different Destinations
a: This study explores preference for familiarity as a key determinant in the travel decision-making process, particularly during the preplanning stage when considering visits to culturally different destinations. This study utilizes quantitative research methods, employing partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze the travel intentions of American millennials toward visiting Thailand. The findings reveal that a preference for familiarity with the destination significantly influences travel intentions, highlighting the impact of past cultural experiences and exposure to destination-related information in forming beliefs and visiting intentions. Additionally, the study suggests that even for travelers seeking novelty destinations, a certain degree of cultural familiarity remains beneficial. These insights provide valuable guidance for organizations aiming to refine their destination marketing strategies by recognizing the role of destination familiarity in travel decisions.
k: destination familiarity; millennials; travel intention; cultural familiarity; destination choice; tourism promotion; Thailand; cultural exposure; novelty seeking

t: Accounting fraud
a: This monograph is intended to inform readers about the detection of financial statement fraud, with a primary focus on the analysis of fraud prediction models. Our intended audience includes academic researchers, doctoral candidates, and graduate students in accounting, finance, and economics with an interest in the empirical study of financial statement fraud. We also hope to inform practitioners and regulators who rely on academic research to support their efforts in detecting or preventing fraudulent financial reporting. Our central interest lies in detecting the most severe form of financial misreporting, that is, intentional financial statement fraud. However, we also consider the broader context in which such behavior occurs. For example, we discuss the incentives and opportunities that more generally give rise to financial misreporting, including less severe forms of misreporting such as accrual and real earnings management, the expanding role of auditors in detecting fraud, and how the combination of reporting incentives, constraints, and trade-offs associated with these less egregious practices can, over time, contribute to a progression along what we term the “road to fraud.” Nonetheless, our primary focus remains on the methodological challenges of fraud prediction, including the limitations of prediction models, the metrics used to assess prediction model performance, and potential avenues for future financial statement fraud prediction research.
k: financial statement fraud; fraud detection; financial misreporting; earnings management; accrual-based earnings management; real earnings management; auditor fraud detection

t: Visibility in the Workplace: A Mixed-Method Study of Visibility Behavior Strategies, Job Performance and Interpersonal Success
a: Visibility in the workplace is widely recognized by scholars and practitioners as a key determinant of career success. Despite its importance for career advancement, visibility in most cases is operationalized as a binary distinction between being present or absent in the physical workplace. In this study, we argue that visibility is a multifaceted construct containing different behavioral strategies that go beyond the pure presence in the workplace. Drawing on a sequential mixed-method design, Study 1 used qualitative interviews (N = 18) with managers from two large German corporations to derive a taxonomy of employees’ visibility behavior strategies. Study 2 (N = 240) tested the differential effects of these strategies on two central indicators of career success – job performance and interpersonal success – and examined whether they explain variance beyond on-site workplace presence. Findings revealed that upward networking, disseminative capacity, and proactive behavior significantly predicted job performance, while helping behavior predicted interpersonal success; the six strategies explained substantial variance in both outcomes beyond on-site presence, which was unrelated to either outcome. These results advance a dual-pathway model of workplace visibility – performance-based and relational – offering a refined conceptualization and practical guidance for managing visibility in hybrid organizational contexts.
k: workplace visibility; career success; employee performance; proactive behavior; helping behavior; dual-pathway model; hybrid work; career development

journal: Cambridge Journal of Regions, Economy and Society
t: Privatisation and remunicipalisation of urban water in Catalonia: between monopolisation, state and the commons
a: We study how the privatisation of urban water is being challenged in Catalonia, which has a high proportion of private management and a high degree of monopolisation in the water contract market, compared to Spain. We use detailed and up-to-date municipal data to study the dynamics of monopolisation and remunicipalisation. We find that remunicipalisation, rather than potential competition for contracts, is a remedy against monopolisation. Inter-municipal cooperation in Catalonia facilitated the implementation of remunicipalisation in smaller municipalities. In addition, we analyse the democratisation of water management following remunicipalisation and find that progress was modest, both in Catalonia and in Spain.
k: urban water; privatization; remunicipalization; inter-municipal cooperation; commons; Catalonia; municipal water management

journal: Journal of International Money and Finance
t: Voting right rotation, speeches, and financial market reactions: Evidence from the U.S. federal open market committee
a: Federal Reserve Bank presidents experience years with and without the right to vote on the U.S. monetary policy committee because of a mechanical voting right rotation scheme. In years presidents vote, their speeches move financial markets less than in years they do not vote. We argue that this vote discount mirrors the way voting status affects presidents’ speech behavior. As speeches given by a president in years with the right to vote are more affected by regional conditions that national markets care less about, markets such as the U.S. Treasury market react less to those speeches.
k: Federal Reserve; Monetary Policy Committee; speech; financial market reactions; Treasury market; monetary policy communication; regional economic conditions

t: Gender pay gap among executive directors: Theoretical insights and perspectives from the critical organizational context of nonlisted government-owned enterprises
a: The gender pay gap, including among executive directors, is a long-standing corporate governance and ethical issue in business and society, with prevailing controversial academic debates calling for further exploration of this context-driven phenomenon. Going beyond the numerous studies on the gender pay gap for private listed enterprises, this study investigates the theoretically salient, critical, yet unexplored organizational context of nonlisted government-owned enterprises. It analyzes a panel dataset spanning 2006–2020, comprising 4,187 executive director observations across 307 German nonlisted government-owned enterprises. The study provides evidence for a pay gap for female executive directors despite specific ethical norms and value expectations in the government-owned enterprise context. Furthermore, in government-owned enterprises with a female board chair, a smaller gender pay gap for female EDs exists. The study enhances the theoretical understanding of the gender pay gap phenomenon in role congruity theory debates. It theoretically and empirically shows the importance of distinguishing between different organizational contexts within a country context when examining gender pay gaps, highlighting the critical and theoretically fruitful organizational context of government-owned enterprises. Furthermore, it indicates that the board chair gender is an important contextual factor for future theoretical debates. Overall, this study opens up the critical organizational context of nonlisted government-owned enterprises as a fertile avenue for future research on the gender pay gap and related theoretical discourses, thereby advancing scholarship and informing practitioners and policymakers.
k: gender pay gap; executive directors; state-owned enterprises; corporate governance; role congruity theory; organizational context; gender equity in leadership; German companies

journal: Journal of Engineering and Technology Management
t: Accelerators revisited: Taking stock and charting the path forward
a: This study provides a comprehensive, updated overview of the literature on accelerators, highlighting their evolving role as cohort-based programs in supporting entrepreneurship and innovation. Accelerators have become central in helping startups overcome financial, skill-related, and legitimacy challenges. However, existing research on the topic remains fragmented. To address this, we conduct a bibliometric analysis of 174 peer-reviewed articles, collected from the Scopus database over the period 2005–2024. The findings reveal five thematic clusters: (1) Accelerators as open innovation tools; (2) Performance measurement and effectiveness; (3) Strategic approaches to startup growth; (4) The role of accelerators in entrepreneurial ecosystems; and (5) Design and evolution of accelerator models. We complement this analysis with an examination of the most cited works from the last five years. By integrating quantitative and qualitative insights, we identify gaps in the accelerator literature associated with these clusters and develop a research agenda structured around five research avenues: (1) Institutional and geographical contexts; (2) Diversity in selection processes; (3) Social and environmental impacts; (4) Collaboration dynamics; and (5) University-based and corporate accelerator roles. The results offer a solid foundation for scholars and practitioners to navigate the evolving landscape of accelerators and their impact on startup ecosystems in a context of post-pandemic environment and ongoing transformation.
k: accelerators; business accelerators; entrepreneurship; innovation; startup growth; entrepreneurial ecosystems; open innovation; corporate accelerators; research agenda; post-pandemic economy

t: Second fiddle strain: How extraversion shapes target CEO turnover following acquisitions
a: After acquisitions, target CEOs are often pushed into a second fiddle role, experiencing a drop in relative standing that contributes to high turnover. These transitions hinge on post-acquisition hierarchies and expectations of deference, making traits linked to dominance consequential. We argue that second fiddle strain arises when trait-based dominance cues clash with these expectations, making the arrangement difficult for both target CEOs and acquiring executives to accept and sustain. Extraverted target CEOs are especially likely to generate such strain because their outgoing and dominant style conflicts with expected restraint. Because acquiring CEOs are central to enacting post-acquisition hierarchies, this strain is shaped by their extraversion. Highly extraverted acquiring CEOs more securely occupy the dominant position and grant greater behavioral latitude, easing constraints on extraverted target CEOs, whereas less extraverted acquiring CEOs rely more on formal authority, tightening these constraints, increasing target CEO turnover. Evidence from US acquisitions supports these arguments.
k: CEO turnover; mergers and acquisitions; extraversion; dominance; deference; formal authority

t: Regularized Generalized Covariance (RGCov) Estimator
a: Summary This paper proposes the Regularized Generalized Covariance (RGCov) estimator, a ridge-type extension of the Generalized Covariance (GCov) estimator for high-dimensional stationary time series. By regularizing the GCov objective function, which involves the inverse of the covariance matrix, RGCov improves numerical stability while preserving positive definiteness. Under suitable conditions, the new estimator is consistent, asymptotically normal, and semi-parametrically efficient. We also extend the GCov specification test and the nonlinear serial dependence (NLSD) test to their regularized versions, both of which are asymptotically chi-square distributed. Simulation studies confirm the reliability of the RGCov and associated tests in high-dimensional settings. In the empirical application, RGCov is used to estimate a mixed causal–noncausal Vector Autoregressive (VAR) model for green energy stocks in the RENIXX index and to construct two bubble-based investment strategies: bubble-riding and bubble-hedging, both of which outperform the benchmark index.
k: Tikhonov regularization; covariance matrix estimation; numerical stability; positive definiteness; consistency; asymptotic normality; specification tests; asset price bubbles

journal: International Journal of Globalisation and Small Business
t: Prioritising barriers to E-commerce adoption in Indian MSMEs: a fuzzy AHP approach
a: : Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are vital to a nations economic output. MSMEs have been the focus of considerable investigation, particularly in the context of disruptions such as digitalisation. Previous studies of MSMEs have not addressed the significant challenges that MSMEs face in adopting E-commerce and digitalisation. This study aims to enumerate, classify, and prioritise barriers obstructing the adoption of E-commerce and digitalisation. Fuzzy AHP, a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) approach, measures and prioritises barriers using sensitivity analysis to enhance robustness. The barriers listed in the regulatory category are the most significant, followed by Legal and Security, Social, Market, Logistics, Technological, and Financial Barriers. Regulations, unpredictable taxation, volatile government regulations, and a lack of standard operating procedures on the E-commerce platform are significant concerns. Technology and financial barriers stand last. It comprehensively categorises and prioritises the barriers, helping to frame policy for MSME growth in India.
k: e-commerce adoption; micro, small and medium enterprises; digitalization; barriers to adoption; fuzzy analytic hierarchy process; regulatory challenges; taxation; cybersecurity; technology barriers; financial barriers; India

t: Comparing risk measures in stochastic equilibrium energy markets
a: This work analyses the impact of incorporating risk measures such as conditional value-at-risk, (second-order) stochastic dominance constraints, and a concave utility function, into equilibrium energy markets. It defines two illustrative problems, with price-making firms facing stochastic demand and stochastic costs respectively, and derives risk-averse equilibrium models based upon these problems. Analytic and numeric results from these models are discussed, highlighting how risk aversion leads to modified expected prices and profits. Specific attention is paid to how the risk measures compare to each other, and how their incorporation alters the complexity of the problem. The problems are defined as mixed complementarity problems using the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, and the potential to recast them to equivalent convex optimization problems is detailed. The work conducts a numerical analysis of the models to gauge the computational expense associated with each risk measure. The impact of incorporating risk measures into equilibrium energy markets is hitherto underexplored in the literature, as are comparative analyses of the various risk measures and their respective advantages in terms of applicability and computational cost. The results indicate that risk aversion causes the variability of profits to decrease regardless of the chosen measure, and highlight the influence which hedging instruments have on risk averse players and price dynamics. They additionally demonstrate that CVaR has a significantly higher computational cost than other risk measures. With increasing stochasticity in energy markets owing to the transition to renewables and geopolitical turmoil, it is imperative that models account for risk-averse decision making accurately, and that the impact of risk measures is understood—this work addresses this gap.
